newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BA, USAir seen locked in risky bluff.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BA, USAir seen locked in risky bluff.

text.p: British Airways share price dipped on Friday on the news that its existing trans-Atlantic partner USAir plans to end their marketing link, thus raising the stakes in BA's ambitious alliance plan with American Airlines.
Although British Airways characterised the move as a kind of minor bluff in a legal spat over USAir's possible status after an eventual BA/American alliance, analysts were less sure.
It revealed deep strains in the USAir-BA relationship, they said, that could end with mixed consequences for both companies.
USAir, in which BA has had a 24.6 percent stake since 1993, said on Thursday that it would end its code-sharing pact and frequent flier programme connection with BA on March 29, 1997.

It laid the blame for this move squarely on BA's plans for a full-scale trans-Atlantic alliance with AMR Corp's American -- an alliance it planned to challenge at a New York court hearing later on Friday.

"I think it's a clear message from USAir to BA and American that it doesn't want to be a junior partner in this, and is ready to consider its other options," said Guy Kekwick, analyst at Lehman Brothers in London.

USAir has not given any public indication of what kind of deal it might be ready to cut with the BA/AA combine, but its chairman Stephen Wolf has dubbed the alliance a "betrayal" and is clearly dissatisfied with vague offers of a marketing link.
British Airways brushed off any possible negative impact from USAir's latest move, with chairman Sir Colin Marshall reportedly calling it "posturing".
But Kekwick and others saw BA taking quite a risk.

"The danger is that if the American deal does not go ahead, the relationship with USAir has deteriorated so far, and BA would then have lost both," said James Halstead, airline analyst at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
This sentiment was certainly seen exerting downward pressure on BA's share price on Friday morning as it fell eight pence to 571p by 1300 GMT, analysts said.

Nevertheless, they added it should also be considered that a clean break with USAir might serve to smooth BA's tricky path to consummating its alliance with American and getting it past the regulators -- thus benefiting the British airline long term.

Since USAir launched its scathing attack on the alliance on July 30 with a "bolt from the blue" lawsuit claiming breach of contract, some observers have seen a chance that USAir may inadvertently be solving BA's potential problem of what to do with two large U.S. partners rather than one.

Getting to this stage would, however, first require American and BA to succeed in gaining U.S. anti-trust immunity for their alliance, which in turn needs a bilateral open-skies deal between the British and the United States governments.
While these issues are likely to be resolved by established channels of politics, lobbying and influence, the USAir dispute may in the end boil down to personalities, analysts said.
Wolf, whose airline has asked the courts to force BA to give up its shareholding and its three board seats, has a reputation as a no-nonsense player with a strong independent streak.

Analysts speculate that he may have already decided not to allow BA to get the upper hand over USAir a second time after the 1993 alliance that brought BA such a lucrative outcome the industry has dubbed the deal BA's "free ride".

Back then, troubled USAir got a welcome $300 million capital injection from BA but gave up its own UK routes, while BA obtained lucrative code-sharing rights in the U.S. that have since earned it good money with little impact on itself.
